title.en: Ricardo and His Adventures: The Frog School and the Seven-Headed Giant
title.zh: 里卡多歷險記：青蛙學堂與七首巨人

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), notes to Tale 49, 'Ricardo and his Adventures', eBook #8299

summary.en: Sent to school, Ricardo studies at the frog-pond and learns to 'read' by croaking; told that 'whenever a body smells bad, you may be sure that it is dead,' he concludes he himself is dead and lies lamenting under a ripe guava he dares not eat. Learning his father was killed by a giant who carried off his sister, he is armed with two bottles of magic water — one making invulnerable, one draining all strength — and a flying saddle from a grateful leper, kills the seven-headed monster, frees the prisoners, and marries Lucia.
summary.zh: 里卡多上學卻在蛙塘『苦讀』，以蛙鳴為誦經；學得『凡發臭者必死』的教訓後，他自認已死，躺在熟番石榴下哀嘆不敢吃。得知父親為七首巨人所殺、妹妹被擄後，他得兩瓶神水（一瓶護體、一瓶奪力）與飛鞍，誅巨人、釋囚徒，娶露西亞為妻。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog tale given in abstract in Fansler's notes to Tale 49 ('If it smells bad, it's dead' droll joined to a giant-slaying tale); archival record.

passages.text: Once there was a widow who had a son named Ricardo. One day the mother said to the boy, 'Ricardo, I want you to go to school, so that you may learn something about our religion.' Ricardo was willing enough, so he took his Catechism and set out — but instead of going to the school, he went to a neighboring pond and listened to the merry croaking of the frogs. When eleven o'clock came, he went home and told his mother about the real school; the poor woman was very happy, thinking that her son was spending his time wisely. Ricardo took great delight in joining the chorus of the frogs, for his mother gave him food as a reward for his diligence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale given in Fansler's notes to Tale 49, 'Ricardo and his Adventures'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One morning the woman asked her son to read his lesson; the boy opened his Catechism and croaked very loudly, and his mother was glad when she heard that her son could croak so well, because she thought that was the way to read the book. As Ricardo was playing with his schoolmates one day, he saw a dead cat; it smelled very bad, so he left the pond and went home: 'Mother, I saw a cat lying near our school. It had a very bad odor.' The mother said, 'My son, remember this: whenever a body smells bad, you may be sure that it is dead' — and Ricardo repeated the words of his mother many times to himself, and learned them by heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale given in Fansler's notes to Tale 49, 'Ricardo and his Adventures'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, when he was on his way to the pond, Ricardo smelled something bad; he looked in every direction, but he could not find anybody: 'Since I cannot find any dead body here, I must be the one who is dead.' He lay down on the ground, and said, 'Ricardo is dead! I cannot eat any more. O how unhappy I am!' While he was lying there, he saw a ripe guava above his head: 'Delicious fruit, you are very fortunate! If I were alive, I would eat you.' He wished to get the fruit, but he dared not do so; after a while, when he could no longer smell the stink, he got up and went home, and told his mother his story.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale given in Fansler's notes to Tale 49, 'Ricardo and his Adventures'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day Ricardo learned from his mother how his father had been killed by a giant who had afterwards carried away his sister; the boy set out in search of the giant. An old man along the way, whom he treated kindly, gave him two bottles of magic water — one that would make invulnerable the man who should drink it, another that would take away all the strength of him on whose head it should be poured; later a leprous old woman to whom he gave some food presented him with a magic saddle that would carry him through the air. So equipped, he soon arrived at the cave of the giant; he succeeded in killing that seven-headed monster and in freeing his sister and many other prisoners. Ten barrels of money were found in the cave; of these, Ricardo took two, the rest he gave to the prisoners he had freed. Later Ricardo married a beautiful woman named Lucia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale given in Fansler's notes to Tale 49, 'Ricardo and his Adventures'; not verbatim.
